evidence_quotes.quote: This paper explores the extent to which Malawi’s national water, sanitation and hygiene (WaSH) sector programmes align with the lived realities of Malawian people through interviews, observations and review of secondary documents.

Fieldwork methods including in-depth and semi-structured interviews, observations, workshops, follow-up interviews and a review of secondary literature were deployed for 33 days (April 14-May 17, 2019). Fifty-two individuals were eventually interviewed through a mix of random and targeted processes from among a range of places, agencies, communities, institutions and the general public across the north, central and southern regions.

Extending public drinking water services to the rural areas was reckoned as economically not viable by the public officials and donors, whose services are mostly tied to the possibility of full cost recovery, implying everyone has to pay for services. This is not possible for the largely low-income rural population.

Legally, the Waterworks Act No. 17 of 1995 statutorily empowered the Water Board to manage the city sewerage system. However, City Councils claim management authority through the Local Government Act of 1998.

Relatively higher cost of services marginalizes certain categories of people including street beggars, homeless people and very low-income earners from having access to toilet facilities when they need it, leaving them with the option of open defecation.

While regulatory enforcement against open defecation is necessary, it however tends to produce the unintended consequence of encouraging poor sanitary practices at the home level in the absence of clear and enforceable guidelines, standard and monitoring mechanisms for building a latrine at homes.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household, community, and public-space drinking water and sanitation service access across urban and rural Malawi, including piped water networks, kiosks, communal taps, boreholes/wells, urban sewerage, household and pay-per-use public latrines, and open defecation.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the paper examines national and local WaSH legal, institutional, regulatory, and donor governance structures in Malawi. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although the paper also critiques macro-level donor 'results and evidence' politics and ministerial coordination, its empirical Results directly examine concrete rule-type mechanisms governing service access: (1) tariff and full cost-recovery rules applied by urban Water Boards, Water Users Associations, and donors (high residential connection/installation fees, monthly tariffs, MK100 kiosk container charges, and full cost-recovery conditions barring rural extension); (2) licensing/outsourcing of municipal and motor-park public latrines to private operators without tariff regulation or operational-hour standards (MK50-MK100 pay-per-use fees); (3) statutory and regulatory jurisdiction conflicts between the Waterworks Act No. 17 of 1995 (Water Boards) and the Local Government Act of 1998 (City Councils) over urban sewerage management; and (4) regulatory enforcement against open defecation (e.g. by forest officers) in the absence of enforceable household latrine standards or subsidies.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary qualitative empirical study based on 33 days of fieldwork (14 April-17 May 2019) across northern, central, and southern Malawi, comprising 52 in-depth and semi-structured interviews, regional stakeholder workshops, direct field observations, and review of secondary documents/statistics.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative and descriptive empirical outcomes on drinking water and sanitation access, supply continuity/regularity (e.g. inability to guarantee 6 hours/day of stable piped supply, multi-day outages, 30-40% non-functional facilities), sewerage coverage (<10% in Blantyre, 5% in Lilongwe), affordability barriers, exclusion of low-income rural/urban households, street beggars, and homeless people from piped water and pay-per-use public latrines, and resulting reliance on unprotected wells (>80% of interviewed Lilongwe households) and open defecation.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (52 interviewees including 22 community/household respondents, 15 public officials, 8 NGO staff, 1 IGO representative, and 6 scientists/students across Lilongwe, Blantyre, Mzuzu, Mzimba, Chikale, Nsungwi, Salima, Chikwawa, and Chilwa; household, community, municipal/utility, and sector levels), rule-type exposures, access/affordability/continuity outcomes, and qualitative fieldwork study design are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Qualitative empirical case study (in-depth and semi-structured interviews, direct field observations, regional stakeholder workshops, and secondary document/statistics review)
population_and_sample: Urban and rural communities and WaSH stakeholders across northern, central, and southern Malawi (Lilongwe, Blantyre, Mzuzu, Mzimba, Chikale, Nsungwi, Salima, Chikwawa, and Chilwa); primary sample of 52 interviewees (22 community/general public members, 15 public officials, 8 NGO representatives, 6 scientists/students, and 1 intergovernmental organisation representative) plus regional workshop participants (units of analysis: household/individual, community, municipal/utility, and national sector institutions).
exposure: WaSH sector governance and rule-type mechanisms in Malawi, including full cost-recovery tariff and connection-fee rules (urban Water Boards, Water Users Associations, donor project viability criteria), unregulated private licensing and pay-per-use pricing of public latrines, statutory jurisdictional overlap over city sewerage (Waterworks Act No. 17 of 1995 vs Local Government Act of 1998), and regulatory enforcement against open defecation without household latrine standards or subsidies.
outcome: Access to improved drinking water and sanitation services, piped supply regularity/continuity, urban sewerage coverage, affordability, cost-based exclusion of low-income and homeless populations from piped water and public latrines, reliance on unprotected wells/surface water, and open defecation or unsafe household pit latrine siting.
rationale: This empirical qualitative socio-legal/governance study meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Drawing on 52 primary interviews, regional workshops, field observations, and secondary sources across Malawi, it investigates household and public-space water and sanitation service access (c1, c3) and reports concrete outcomes on access, supply continuity, sewerage coverage, affordability, and exclusion (c4, c5, c6). Alongside broader analysis of donor results-oriented governance, the empirical findings directly examine rule-type legal, regulatory, and tariff mechanisms governing access—specifically full cost-recovery rules and connection/kiosk tariffs, unregulated private licensing and user charges for municipal/motor-park latrines, statutory mandate conflicts between Water Boards and City Councils under the Waterworks Act 1995 and Local Government Act 1998, and enforcement against open defecation without accompanying standards or subsidies (c2). Per protocol safeguards, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for systematic review inclusion.
